prompt: A technician needs to copy a 7 GB video file to a USB flash drive that must work on both Windows and macOS. The copy fails with "file too large."

options.text: Reformat the drive as APFS, Apple's native format, with no file size limit on macOS
Reformat the drive as NTFS, which handles large files and is read-write on Windows but only read-only by default on macOS
Reformat the drive as exFAT, which has no 4 GB file limit and is read-write on both systems
Compress the file with a zip tool until it is under 4 GB, if the video shrinks enough

explanation: The drive is almost certainly FAT32, which has a 4 GB maximum file size. exFAT removes that limit and is read-write on both Windows and macOS. macOS cannot write NTFS by default, and Windows cannot read APFS without extra software.

prompt: A domain user's newly assigned drive mappings and desktop settings have not appeared, although other users in the same OU have them. The technician wants to apply the policy immediately and then confirm which policies applied.

options.text: net user, then whoami, which list account details and the signed-in identity but do not refresh or report Group Policy settings
gpupdate /force to reapply policy now, then gpresult /r to confirm which policies applied to the user and computer
ipconfig /renew, then nslookup, which refresh the IP lease and test name resolution, not Group Policy
sfc /scannow, then chkdsk, which check system files and the disk but do not apply Group Policy

explanation: gpupdate /force reapplies all Group Policy settings, and gpresult /r reports which policies applied to the user and computer. The other commands repair files, check disks, or deal with networking and accounts, not policy.

prompt: A Linux administrator must let the owner read, write, and execute a script, while the group and everyone else can only read and execute it.

options.text: chmod 777 script.sh, which gives the owner what is needed but also gives group and others write permission
chown 755 script.sh, which looks like the correct mode but chown sets file ownership rather than permissions
chmod 644 script.sh, which lets the owner read and write and everyone else read, but nobody can run the script
chmod 755 script.sh

explanation: Read is 4, write is 2, and execute is 1. Owner rwx is 7, and group and others r-x is 5 each, so 755. 777 gives everyone write access, 644 removes execute, and chown changes ownership rather than permissions.

prompt: A shared folder grants Everyone "Full Control" at the share level. The NTFS permissions give the Sales group "Read." A Sales user tries to save a file to the share over the network.

options.text: The save succeeds because share permissions allow Full Control to Everyone, so NTFS Read is not consulted
The save fails because the most restrictive of the share and NTFS permissions applies, leaving the user with Read only
The save succeeds because NTFS permissions apply only to users signed in at the machine
The save fails because the Everyone entry overrides the Sales group and removes all write access

explanation: Network access passes through both share and NTFS permissions, and the effective permission is the more restrictive of the two. Read beats Full Control here. NTFS permissions apply both locally and over the network.

prompt: A technician has confirmed that a home user's PC shows malware symptoms and has disconnected it from the network. What should happen next in CompTIA's malware removal procedure?

options.text: Reimage the PC from a clean image right away, because a confirmed infection cannot be trusted
Educate the end user about safe browsing and email habits, so the infection is not repeated
Schedule scans and run updates, so definitions are current and later scans find leftover traces
Disable System Restore in Windows so that infected restore points cannot bring the malware back after cleanup

explanation: The order is investigate and verify, quarantine, disable System Restore, remediate (update anti-malware, scan and remove, reimage if needed), schedule scans and updates, re-enable System Restore and create a restore point, then educate the user. System Restore is disabled so infected restore points cannot bring the malware back.

prompt: A clinic is retiring laptops with SSDs that held patient data. It needs a method that makes the data unrecoverable and gives auditors proof.

options.text: Delete the patient folders and empty the Recycle Bin, which removes file entries but leaves the data recoverable with common tools
Degauss the SSDs with a strong magnet, which erases magnetic platters but has no effect on flash memory
Use a certified vendor to physically shred the drives and issue a certificate of destruction as audit evidence
Run a standard format on each drive, which rebuilds the file system but leaves the data recoverable with freely available tools

explanation: Shredding destroys any media, and the certificate is the audit evidence. Degaussing works only on magnetic media, so it does nothing to SSDs. A standard format or deleting files leaves data recoverable.

prompt: Right after a graphics driver update, a Windows PC shows a blue screen during every normal startup. It starts normally in Safe Mode.

options.text: Reinstall Windows from scratch, which would remove the faulty driver but also erases installed applications and settings
Run chkdsk /r to scan the disk for bad sectors, which would help if the cause were disk damage rather than the driver
Boot into Safe Mode and roll back the graphics driver, the least disruptive fix for the cause
Replace the graphics card, though the timing points to the driver

explanation: The timing points to the driver, and Safe Mode loads only basic drivers, which is why it boots there. Rolling back the driver is the least disruptive fix that addresses the cause. Reinstalling Windows or replacing hardware is premature.

prompt: A user's phone suddenly shows many full-screen ads, uses far more mobile data than usual, and the battery drains quickly. The user recently installed a flashlight app from a website link rather than the official store.

options.text: Remove the sideloaded app, scan the device, and factory reset if symptoms continue
Reset network settings, which clears saved Wi-Fi and cellular configuration but leaves the offending app installed
Turn off location services for all apps, which reduces some tracking but does not stop ads or background data use
Replace the battery, since fast drain is a hardware fault and ads and data use are separate matters

explanation: An app from an unofficial source, along with ads, high data use, and battery drain, points to adware or other malware. Remove the app first, then scan. A factory reset (after backing up data) is the fallback. The battery and network settings are symptoms, not the cause.

prompt: A company runs a full backup on Sunday and differential backups Monday through Saturday. The server fails on Thursday morning.

options.text: Sunday's full plus Monday's differential, which holds only the first day of changes
Sunday's full only
Sunday's full plus Wednesday's differential
Wednesday's differential only

explanation: Each differential contains every change since the last full, so only the latest differential is needed with the full. If these had been incrementals, every one since Sunday would be required, in order.

prompt: A help desk technician wants to paste a user's error log, which includes the user's name, email, and an internal server password, into a free public AI chatbot to get help diagnosing it.

options.text: Do not paste sensitive data into a public AI tool; remove personal and secret data or use an approved private tool, and verify any answer
Paste it, but add a request in the prompt asking the chatbot not to store or learn from the content that is entered
Email the log to a personal account and use the chatbot from a home computer, so the company network is not involved
Paste it as written, because AI tools give accurate results and so the full log is needed to get a correct diagnosis

explanation: Public AI tools may keep or train on what is entered, so pasting PII and credentials is a data security and privacy failure. Organizational AI policy and approved private tools exist for this reason. AI output can also be inaccurate or hallucinated, so any suggested fix must be checked before it is used.
